title: Most Expensive Part of an HVAC System to Replace
h1: What Is the Most Expensive Part of an HVAC System to Replace?
description: The compressor is usually the most expensive HVAC part to replace, followed by coils and heat exchangers. Learn what causes failures and how to avoid them.
quick_answer: The compressor is usually the most expensive single part to replace in an air conditioner or heat pump. Evaporator and condenser coils come next, and on a gas furnace, the heat exchanger is the costliest part. When one of these fails on an older system, replacing the whole unit often makes more sense than the repair.
body:
Most HVAC repairs are small: a capacitor, a contactor, a flame sensor or a clogged drain line. But a few parts are expensive because they're complex, labor-intensive or involve handling refrigerant. Knowing which ones they are helps you understand a repair quote and decide whether to fix or replace.

Why is the compressor so expensive?

The compressor is the heart of an AC or heat pump. It pressurizes refrigerant and pumps it through the system. Replacing it means recovering the refrigerant, cutting out and brazing in the new compressor, replacing the filter drier, pulling a vacuum and recharging the system. That's a lot of skilled labor on top of the part itself.

Common causes of compressor failure include:

  • Low refrigerant from a leak, which makes the compressor overheat
  • Dirty outdoor coils that force it to run hot
  • Electrical problems, like a failing capacitor or burned contacts
  • Restricted airflow from dirty filters or blocked ducts
  • Wrong refrigerant charge from the start
  • Age and normal wear

What other HVAC parts are costly to replace?

Evaporator coil

The indoor coil sits above or next to the furnace or air handler. Coils can develop small refrigerant leaks over time, especially when exposed to household chemicals or poor airflow. Replacing one involves refrigerant work and sometimes modifying the cabinet to fit.

Condenser coil

The outdoor coil wraps around the condenser unit. In coastal neighborhoods, salt air can corrode the thin aluminum fins and copper tubing. A badly corroded coil often means the whole outdoor unit is near the end.

Furnace heat exchanger

The heat exchanger separates the flames from the air that goes into your home. If it cracks, combustion gases, including carbon monoxide, can mix with household air. A cracked heat exchanger is a safety issue, and the furnace should not be run until it's addressed. On an older furnace, replacement is usually the better choice.

Blower motor and control board

These are less costly than the parts above, but variable-speed blower motors and control boards on newer systems can still be significant repairs.

When does it make sense to replace instead of repair?

A big repair on a young system under warranty is usually worth doing, since the part may be covered and you'll only pay labor. On an older system, think about these questions:

  • Is the system more than about 10 to 12 years old?
  • Does it use R-22 refrigerant, which is no longer produced?
  • Have you had other major repairs recently?
  • Is the repair a large share of what a new system would cost?
  • Are comfort and efficiency already slipping?

If you answer yes to several, putting the money toward a new system is often the smarter move. You'll also get a fresh warranty and better efficiency.

How can you protect the expensive parts?

  1. Change filters on schedule so the coil and blower get proper airflow.
  2. Keep the outdoor unit clean and clear. Rinse salt and dust from the coil and keep plants back.
  3. Get an annual tune-up. Technicians catch weak capacitors, low refrigerant and dirty coils before they damage the compressor.
  4. Fix refrigerant leaks properly. Topping off a leaking system over and over can cost more over time than repairing the leak.
  5. Install surge protection to protect compressors and control boards from power spikes.

What should you do if you suspect a major failure?

Signs include an outdoor unit that hums but won't start, warm air from the vents, breakers that keep tripping, or ice on the refrigerant lines. On a furnace, watch for soot, a yellow or flickering flame, or a carbon monoxide alarm. If a CO alarm sounds, get everyone out and call 911. If you smell gas, leave and call the gas utility from outside.

For anything else, turn the system off and have it checked. Our HVAC repair technicians will diagnose the problem, explain whether repair or replacement makes more sense and give you a free estimate on a replacement if you need one.
faqs: Is a compressor covered under warranty?

Many manufacturers cover compressors for several years, sometimes longer if the equipment was registered. Parts warranties often don't cover labor or refrigerant, which can be a large part of the bill. Check your paperwork or ask your technician to look up the serial number.
Can a cracked heat exchanger be repaired?

Generally no. Manufacturers and safety standards call for replacing the heat exchanger or the furnace. Patching it isn't considered safe. On an older furnace, replacing the whole unit is usually the better value.
How do I know if my AC compressor is failing?

Warning signs include warm air from the vents, a loud clanking or humming outdoor unit, breakers tripping when the AC starts and the outdoor fan running while the compressor stays silent. A technician can test it to confirm.
